claim: C. elegans MUT-7 shares 29% sequence identity with the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain of human WRN.
source: C. elegans MUT-7 shares 29% sequence identity with the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain of human WRN (Ketting et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ketting et al., 1999, which provides the sequence identity comparison.

claim: C. elegans CeWRN-1 shows 43% sequence identity with the helicase domain of human WRN.
source: In C. elegans, CeWRN-1 shows 43% sequence identity with the helicase domain of human WRN (Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2004, which provides the sequence identity comparison.

claim: Loss of CeWRN-1 causes decreased lifespan and pharyngeal clogging in C. elegans.
source: Loss of CeWRN-1 seems to cause several progeroid phenotypes, such as decreased lifespan and pharyngeal clogging in the worm head (Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2004, which describes these phenotypes.

claim: WS patients have been observed to show brain atrophy.
source: WS patients have recently been observed to show a brain atrophy (Goto et al., 2013; Lebel and Monnat, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goto et al., 2013 and Lebel and Monnat, 2018.

claim: Prolonged odor exposure in the absence of food causes C. elegans to ignore a previously attractive odor.
source: Prolonged odor exposure in the absence of food causes the animals to ignore a previously attractive odor (Colbert and Bargmann, 1997; L'Etoile et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colbert and Bargmann, 1997 and L'Etoile et al., 2002.

claim: Behavioral plasticity in C. elegans results from changes within an AWC neuron driving EGL-4 into the nucleus.
source: This behavioral plasticity results from changes within an AWC neuron itself driving a cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG), EGL-4, into the nucleus (Lee et al., 2010a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010a.

claim: Neuronal plasticity requires a reduction in the mRNA expression levels of guanylyl cyclase ODR-1.
source: A feedback mechanism involved in the process of neuronal plasticity requires a reduction in the mRNA expression levels of a membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase, ODR-1 (L'Etoile and Bargmann, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to L'Etoile and Bargmann, 2000.

claim: Transcriptional silencing is mediated by loading HPL-2 onto the odr-1 locus.
source: Transcriptional silencing is mediated by loading the heterochromatin-binding protein HPL-2 (an HP1 homolog) onto the odr-1 locus (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Juang et al., 2013.

claim: The assembly of heterochromatin complexes is directed by an increase in odr-1 22G siRNA.
source: The assembly of heterochromatin complexes is directed by an increase in the odr-1 small interfering RNA (siRNA), consisting of 22 nucleotides starting with a 5′ guanosine (22G), whose synthesis requires the 3′−5′ exonuclease activity of MUT-7 in butanone-trained animals (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Juang et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of functional mut-7 ortholog in Arabidopsis thaliana leads to defective post-transcriptional gene silencing.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, loss of the functional mut-7 ortholog encoding a WS-like exonuclease (WEX) leads to defective post-transcriptional gene silencing (Glazov et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glazov et al., 2003.

claim: MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 are required for animals to learn to ignore butanone after odor training.
source: Strains that lacked MUT-7 or CeWRN-1 were analyzed in the chemotaxis assay, and we found that their odor-trained CI was not only greater than half of the naïve CI but also significantly differed from the CIs of odor-trained wild-type animals (Figure 1B, lower figure), suggesting that MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 are required for animals to learn.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 act in the same pathway in AWC neurons to promote olfactory learning.
source: To examine whether MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 act in the same genetic pathway, we generated mut-7;Cewrn-1 double mutants and found that the ability of the double-mutant animals to alter their response to butanone was similar to that of single-mutant animals (Figure 1B, lower). Thus, the data indicate that MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 act in the same pathway in AWC neurons to promote olfactory learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis data from double mutant analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mut-7(ne4255) allele with E437K mutation reduces the activity of the 3′−5′ exonuclease.
source: An allele of mut-7(ne4255) with a missense mutation at E437K has been predicted to reduce the activity of the 3′−5′ exonuclease by interrupting the predicted Mg2+ binding domain (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2009, which predicts the effect of this mutation.

claim: mut-7(ne4255) mutant animals are defective in butanone chemotaxis.
source: mut-7(ne4255) mutant animals were shown to be defective in butanone chemotaxis (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Worms carrying the W812 Amber mutation in MUT-7 showed reduced 22G RNA levels.
source: Worms carrying the W812 Amber mutation in MUT-7 showed reduced 22G RNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: mut-7(pk204) mutants are able to show chemotaxis toward butanone but unable to learn to ignore this odor after it was paired with starvation.
source: Worms carrying the W812 Amber mutation in MUT-7 showed reduced 22G RNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and although they were able to show chemotaxis toward butanone, they were unable to learn to ignore this odor after it was paired with starvation (Figure 1C; Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and cited from Juang et al., 2013.

claim: The expression of GFP-MUT-7 in AWC cells restored odor learning in mut-7(pk204) mutant animals.
source: We previously found that the expression of MUT-7 with GFP appended to its N-terminus (GFP-MUT-7 in Figure 2A, upper) specifically in AWC cells restored odor learning in mut-7(pk204) mutant animals (Figure 2B, fourth pair).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of GFP-MUT-7 in AWC restored odr-1 22G RNA levels in mut-7(pk204) odor-trained worms.
source: The expression of GFP-MUT-7 in AWC also restored odr-1 22G RNA levels in mut-7(pk204) odor-trained worms (Figure 2C, third dataset) (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and cited from Juang et al., 2013.

claim: Prolonged odor exposure decreased odr-1 mRNA levels in wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, we used quantitative real-time PCR to probe odr-1 mRNA and found that prolonged odor exposure decreased odr-1 mRNA levels in wild-type animals, while odr-1 mRNA levels were insensitive to odor exposure in mut-7(pk204) mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: odr-1 mRNA levels were insensitive to odor exposure in mut-7(pk204) mutant animals.
source: Indeed, we used quantitative real-time PCR to probe odr-1 mRNA and found that prolonged odor exposure decreased odr-1 mRNA levels in wild-type animals, while odr-1 mRNA levels were insensitive to odor exposure in mut-7(pk204) mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP-tagged ODR-1 was concentrated in the flattened ciliated end of the AWC neuron.
source: Furthermore, we used a CRISPR-Cas9 system to generate an integrated line expressing ODR-1::GFP under the control of the endogenous odr-1 promoter. GFP-tagged ODR-1 was concentrated in the flattened ciliated end of the AWC neuron (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of ODR-1::GFP in naïve wild-type animals was significantly brighter than in odor-trained wild-type animals.
source: The fluorescence intensity in naïve wild-type animals was significantly brighter than the fluorescence of GFP in odor-trained wild-type animals (Figure 2D, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No significant difference in ODR-1::GFP expression induced by odor exposure was observed in mut-7(pk204) mutants.
source: In contrast, no significant difference in GFP expression induced by odor exposure was observed in the mut-7(pk204) mutants (Figure 2D, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MUT-7 is required in the synthesis of odr-1 22G RNA after prolonged odor treatment to downregulate the expression of both odr-1 mRNA and ODR-1 protein.
source: These results confirm that MUT-7 is required in the synthesis of odr-1 22G RNA after prolonged odor treatment to specifically downregulate the expression of both the odr-1 mRNA and the ODR-1 protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results from RT-qPCR and fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: Animals in which MUT-7 was restricted to the cytoplasm showed an increase in odr-1.7 22G RNA levels to the same level found in wild type when odor trained.
source: We found that animals in which MUT-7 was restricted to the cytoplasm (CterGFP-MUT-7) showed an increase in the odr-1.7 22G RNA levels to the same level found in the wild type when they were odor trained (Figure 2C, first versus fourth datasets).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Animals with cytoplasm-restricted MUT-7 exhibited wild-type levels of odr-1.7 22G RNA but were not able to learn as well as wild types.
source: This was interesting because although they exhibited wild-type levels of odr-1.7 22G RNA, these animals were not able to learn as well as the wild types (Figure 2B, first versus fifth pairs of bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined data from RT-qPCR (Figure 2C) and behavioral assays (Figure 2B).

claim: Restricting MUT-7 to the nucleus blocked the odor-dependent increases in both 22G RNA and learning.
source: By contrast, restricting MUT-7 to the nucleus (NLS-GFP-MUT-7) blocked the odor-dependent increases in both 22G RNA (Figure 2C, first versus fifth dataset) and learning (Figure 2B, first versus sixth pairs of bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined data from RT-qPCR (Figure 2C) and behavioral assays (Figure 2B).

claim: Expressing both CterGFP-MUT-7 and NLS-GFP-MUT-7 in mut-7(pk204) mutants restored both 22G RNA levels and odor learning.
source: Importantly, each version of MUT-7 was functional, as expressing both CterGFP-MUT-7 and NLS-GFP-MUT-7 in the mut-7(pk204) mutants restored both 22G RNA levels and odor learning (Figure 2B, seventh pair of bars, and Figure 2C, sixth dataset).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined data from RT-qPCR (Figure 2C) and behavioral assays (Figure 2B).

claim: 22G RNA production is not sufficient to cause odor learning.
source: Thus, 22G RNA production is not sufficient to cause odor learning, and MUT-7 must perform an additional role in the nucleus, because when it is restricted from the nucleus, animals do not learn.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cytoplasmic MUT-7 produces 22G RNA but does not fully restore learning.

claim: MUT-7 must perform an additional role in the nucleus for odor learning to occur.
source: Thus, 22G RNA production is not sufficient to cause odor learning, and MUT-7 must perform an additional role in the nucleus, because when it is restricted from the nucleus, animals do not learn.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that nuclear MUT-7 is required for learning even when 22G RNA is produced.

claim: Cytoplasmic MUT-7 functions in the small RNA synthesis process.
source: Taken together, our behavioral and RT-qPCR results indicate that cytoplasmic MUT-7 may function in the small RNA synthesis process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and RT-qPCR results.

claim: MUT-7 acts in a different way in the nucleus compared to the cytoplasm.
source: These results also provide insight that MUT-7 acts in a different way in the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that nuclear and cytoplasmic MUT-7 have distinct functions.

claim: The two pools of MUT-7 must act in coordination to promote olfactory learning.
source: Moreover, the two pools of MUT-7 must (indirectly) act in coordination to promote olfactory learning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both nuclear and cytoplasmic MUT-7 are required for full learning.

claim: Asymmetric expression of STR-2 was observed in more than 96% of animals expressing CterGFP-MUT-7 or NLS-GFP-MUT-7.
source: To determine whether the various versions of MUT-7 affect this cell fate, STR-2-driven DsRed fluorescence was expressed in CterGFP-MUT-7 or NLS-GFP-MUT-7 transgenic animals, and asymmetric expression of STR-2 was observed in more than 96% of tested animals (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The impairment of behavioral plasticity in adult animals carrying CterGFP-MUT-7 or NLS-GFP-MUT-7 is not due to changes in cell fate.
source: This result suggests that the impairment of behavioral plasticity in adult animals carrying CterGFP-MUT-7 or NLS-GFP-MUT-7 is not due to changes in cell fate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cell fate is normal in these animals.

claim: Mutations in the PKG consensus sites of MUT-7 caused defects in odor learning.
source: Mutations in the PKG consensus sites of MUT-7 caused defects in odor learning (Figure 3A; Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and cited from Juang et al., 2013.

claim: MUT-7 acts downstream of nuclear EGL-4.
source: Our previous genetic epistasis experiments indicated that MUT-7 acts downstream of nuclear EGL-4 (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Juang et al., 2013, which describes genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Only 1% of buffer-trained animals showed a reconstituted BiFC fluorescent signal between MUT-7 and EGL-4 in the AWC nucleus.
source: We observed that only 1% of buffer-trained animals showed a reconstituted fluorescent signal in the AWC nucleus and that this percentage rose to 75% after prolonged odor training (Figure 3B and C, first row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: 75% of odor-trained animals showed a reconstituted BiFC fluorescent signal between MUT-7 and EGL-4 in the AWC nucleus.
source: We observed that only 1% of buffer-trained animals showed a reconstituted fluorescent signal in the AWC nucleus and that this percentage rose to 75% after prolonged odor training (Figure 3B and C, first row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The BiFC signal between MUT-7 and EGL-4 in each butanone-trained animal was seen in only one AWC neuron.
source: Importantly, the BiFC signal in each butanone-trained animal was seen in only one AWC neuron.
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC microscopy observations.

claim: Butanone is sensed by only one AWC neuron.
source: This reflects the fact that butanone is sensed by only one AWC (Wes and Bargmann, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wes and Bargmann, 2001.

claim: 86% of odor-trained animals expressing NLS::EGL-4 and MUT-7 exhibited the BiFC signal.
source: In addition, we tested constitutively nuclear EGL-4 tagged with the Venus C-terminus (NLS::EGL-4) in naïve animals expressing MUT-7 tagged with the Venus N-terminus, and 86% of odor-trained animals exhibited the BiFC signal (Figure 3C, third row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EGL-4 associates either directly or in a protein complex with MUT-7 in the AWC nucleus of odor-trained worms.
source: These results indicate that EGL-4 associates either directly or in a protein complex with MUT-7 in the AWC nucleus of odor-trained worms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results showing interaction between EGL-4 and MUT-7.

claim: Nonphosphorylatable forms of MUT-7 with all seven PKG phosphorylation sites mutated to alanine failed to reconstitute the BiFC signal with EGL-4.
source: Thus, we performed a similar BiFC analysis with MUT-7 variants in which all seven of the predicted PKG phosphorylation sites were mutated to nonphosphorylatable alanine residues (Figure 3A). These nonphosphorylatable forms of MUT-7 failed to reconstitute the BiFC signal (Figure 3C, second and fourth rows).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The single S883A mutation in MUT-7 was sufficient to block BiFC fluorescence with EGL-4.
source: The single S883A mutation (at a site deleted in the pk204 allele of mut-7) was sufficient to block BiFC fluorescence (Figure 3C, sixth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The phosphorylated form of MUT-7 is bound by EGL-4 in the AWC nucleus.
source: Taken together, these data lead us to propose that the phosphorylated form of MUT-7 is bound by EGL-4 in the AWC nucleus and that EGL-4 kinase may be responsible for phosphorylating MUT-7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results showing that phosphorylation sites are required for the interaction.

claim: EGL-4 kinase may be responsible for phosphorylating MUT-7.
source: Taken together, these data lead us to propose that the phosphorylated form of MUT-7 is bound by EGL-4 in the AWC nucleus and that EGL-4 kinase may be responsible for phosphorylating MUT-7.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference from BiFC results.

claim: A point mutation in MUT-7 (S516A) does not affect learning.
source: As a control, a point mutation in MUT-7 (S516A) that does not affect learning (Figure 3A, fifth pair for behavior) (Juang et al., 2013) was shown to not disrupt BiFC between EGL-4 and MUT-7 (Figure 3C, fifth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A and cited from Juang et al., 2013.

claim: The S516A mutation in MUT-7 does not disrupt BiFC between EGL-4 and MUT-7.
source: As a control, a point mutation in MUT-7 (S516A) that does not affect learning (Figure 3A, fifth pair for behavior) (Juang et al., 2013) was shown to not disrupt BiFC between EGL-4 and MUT-7 (Figure 3C, fifth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only 11% of odor-trained transgenic animals expressing MUT-7(W812Amber) showed the BiFC signal with EGL-4.
source: We found that only 11% of odor-trained transgenic animals showed the BiFC signal (Figure 3C, seventh row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The production of odr-1 22G RNA by processes involving MUT-7 in the cytoplasm is required for the association between EGL-4 and MUT-7 in the AWC nucleus.
source: This result suggests that the production of odr-1 22G RNA by processes that involve MUT-7 in the cytoplasm is required for the association between EGL-4 and MUT-7 in the AWC nucleus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results with the W812Amber mutant.

claim: The cytoplasmic and nuclear pools of MUT-7 do not have to move between compartments to promote odor learning.
source: We have presented evidence that the cytoplasmic and nuclear pools of MUT-7 do not have to move between the compartments to promote odor learning (Figure 2B; the co-expression of NLS-GFP-MUT-7 and CterGFP-MUT-7 in mut-7(pk204) animals rescues mut-7 learning defects).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NRDE-3 shuttles 22G siRNA from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in the nuclear RNA silencing pathway.
source: One candidate potentially mediating this process is the Argonaut NRDE-3, which shuttles 22G siRNA from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in the nuclear RNA silencing pathway (Guang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guang et al., 2008.

claim: odr-1 22G RNAs are loaded onto NRDE-3 in butanone odor-trained worms.
source: A previous coimmunoprecipitation analysis revealed that odr-1 22G RNAs are loaded onto NRDE-3 in butanone odor-trained worms (Juang et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Juang et al., 2013, which describes coimmunoprecipitation results.

claim: The BiFC signal between MUT-7 and EGL-4 was not detected in nrde-3(gg66) mutant animals in either naïve or odor-trained conditions.
source: We expressed MUT-7 tagged with the Venus N-terminus and EGL-4 tagged with the Venus C-terminus in nrde-3(gg66) mutant animals lacking NRDE-3. We found that the BiFC signal was not detected in either naïve or odor-trained transgenic worms (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, first row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 86% of odor-trained wild-type worms co-expressing NLS::EGL-4 and constitutively nuclear MUT-7 showed a BiFC signal.
source: Furthermore, we observed that 86% of odor-trained wild-type worms co-expressing NLS::EGL-4 and constitutively nuclear MUT-7 tagged with the Venus N-terminus (NLS::MUT-7) showed a BiFC signal (Figure 3C, last row)
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only 5% of odor-trained nrde-3(gg66) mutant worms expressing NLS::EGL-4 and NLS::MUT-7 showed a BiFC signal.
source: but that only 5% of odor-trained nrde-3(gg66) mutant worms expressing the same constructs showed a BiFC signal (Figure 4D, first row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The import of 22G RNAs into the nucleus via NRDE-3 is required for the association between nuclear MUT-7 and EGL-4.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the import of 22G RNAs into the nucleus via NRDE-3 is required for the association between nuclear MUT-7 and EGL-4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in nrde-3 mutants.

claim: Strains lacking CeWRN-1 were unable to learn to ignore butanone after training.
source: Olfactory behavioral analysis revealed that strains lacking CeWRN-1 were unable to learn to ignore butanone after training (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GFP expression under the control of the Cewrn-1 promoter showed a signal in many cells, including the pair of AWC neurons.
source: The expression pattern of CeWRN-1 has not been characterized in vivo, so we placed GFP expression under the control of the Cewrn-1 promoter and observed a GFP signal in many cells, including the pair of AWC neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of CeWRN-1 protein in AWCs rescued the learning defects of the Cewrn-1(gk99) mutant.
source: To determine whether CeWRN-1 acts in AWC neurons to regulate odor sensing and learning, the CeWRN-1 protein was expressed in AWCs and rescued the learning defects of the Cewrn-1(gk99) mutant (Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GFP-tagged CeWRN-1 stained the AWC nucleus.
source: Furthermore, GFP-tagged CeWRN-1 stained the AWC nucleus (Figure 4B, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CeWRN-1 acts within AWC neurons to promote olfactory plasticity.
source: These data indicate that CeWRN-1 acts within AWC neurons to promote olfactory plasticity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments and localization data.

claim: The wild-type pattern of asymmetric STR-2 expression was observed in all tested Cewrn-1 mutant animals.
source: This is unlikely to be due to a change in AWC cell fate because the wild-type pattern of asymmetric STR-2 expression was observed in all tested animals (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: GFP-tagged EGL-4 entered the nucleus of AWC neurons in Cewrn-1(gk99) animals that had been trained with butanone.
source: We found that GFP-tagged EGL-4 entered the nucleus of AWC neurons in Cewrn-1(gk99) animals that had been trained with butanone (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: CeWRN-1 does not regulate EGL-4 nuclear entry.
source: Thus, CeWRN-1 does not regulate EGL-4 nuclear entry.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EGL-4 enters the nucleus in Cewrn-1 mutants.

claim: Less than 2% of transgenic animals expressing CeWRN-1 and EGL-4 BiFC constructs showed a fluorescent signal under either naïve or trained conditions.
source: To test this hypothesis, we appended the N-terminal half of Venus to CeWRN-1 and expressed this construct in a strain-expressing EGL-4 tagged with the C-terminal half of Venus. Less than 2% of transgenic animals under either naïve or trained conditions showed a fluorescent signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, second row)
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CeWRN-1 and EGL-4 do not interact directly.
source: Less than 2% of transgenic animals under either naïve or trained conditions showed a fluorescent signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, second row), suggesting that the CeWRN-1 and EGL-4 do not interact directly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of BiFC signal.

claim: 46% of odor-trained worms co-expressing CeWRN-1 and MUT-7 BiFC constructs showed the BiFC signal.
source: To explore whether nematode MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 could interact, the BiFC constructs for CeWRN-1 and MUT-7 were co-expressed in wild-type animals, and 46% of odor-trained worms showed the BiFC signal, in contrast to <4% of buffer-trained control worms (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, third row; Figure 4C, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Less than 4% of buffer-trained control worms co-expressing CeWRN-1 and MUT-7 BiFC constructs showed the BiFC signal.
source: To explore whether nematode MUT-7 and CeWRN-1 could interact, the BiFC constructs for CeWRN-1 and MUT-7 were co-expressed in wild-type animals, and 46% of odor-trained worms showed the BiFC signal, in contrast to <4% of buffer-trained control worms (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, third row; Figure 4C, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 3% of naïve and odor-trained nrde-3(gg99) mutants expressing CeWRN-1 and MUT-7 BiFC constructs exhibited the BiFC signal.
source: In addition, the same BiFC constructs were expressed in nrde-3(gg99) mutants, and only 3% of naïve and odor-rained worms exhibited the BiFC signal (Figure 4D, second row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CeWRN-1 may associate with nuclear MUT-7 in the presence of NRDE-3.
source: These results indicate that CeWRN-1 may associate with nuclear MUT-7 in the presence of NRDE-3 and that they may mediate olfactory learning together.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in wild-type and nrde-3 mutant backgrounds.

claim: Very few naïve or odor-trained animals expressing MUT-7 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs showed BiFC.
source: To distinguish between these possibilities, we first asked whether MUT-7 and HPL-2 are in close enough association in the nucleus to reconstitute fluorescence (BiFC). We found that very few naïve or odor-trained animals showed BiFC (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, fourth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MUT-7 and HPL-2 are unlikely to be associated even after odor training.
source: Thus, MUT-7 and HPL-2 are unlikely to be associated even after odor training.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of BiFC signal between MUT-7 and HPL-2.

claim: 67% of odor-trained hpl-2 null animals showed BiFC between EGL-4 and MUT-7.
source: Second, we asked if the EGL-4-MUT-7 association requires HPL-2. We found that, in hpl-2 null animals, 67% of odor-trained animals showed BiFC, in contrast to only 1% of naïve animals (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, fifth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HPL-2 does not exist in a complex with MUT-7.
source: Thus, neither does HPL-2 exist in a complex with MUT-7 nor is it required to promote the association between MUT-7 and EGL-4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in hpl-2 mutants.

claim: HPL-2 is not required to promote the association between MUT-7 and EGL-4.
source: Thus, neither does HPL-2 exist in a complex with MUT-7 nor is it required to promote the association between MUT-7 and EGL-4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in hpl-2 mutants.

claim: 91.5% of odor-trained worms expressing HIS-71 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs showed BiFC.
source: When we expressed HIS-71 tagged with the Venus N-terminus and HPL-2 tagged with the Venus C-terminus in wild-type animals, we found that 91.5% of odor-trained worms showed BiFC, in contrast to a background rate of 11.6% in naïve worms (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, sixth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 11.6% of naïve worms expressing HIS-71 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs showed BiFC.
source: When we expressed HIS-71 tagged with the Venus N-terminus and HPL-2 tagged with the Venus C-terminus in wild-type animals, we found that 91.5% of odor-trained worms showed BiFC, in contrast to a background rate of 11.6% in naïve worms (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, sixth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Odor training increases the association between HPL-2 and H3.3.
source: Thus, odor training increases the association between HPL-2 and H3.3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased BiFC signal in odor-trained animals.

claim: Less than 4% of either naïve or odor-trained mut-7(pk204) mutant animals expressing HIS-71 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs exhibited the BiFC signal.
source: To determine whether MUT-7 is required for the increased association, the same set of BiFC constructs was expressed in the mut-7(pk204) mutant background, and less than 4% of either naïve or odor-trained animals exhibited the BiFC signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, seventh row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MUT-7 is required for the formation of the HPL-2-H3 complex in odor-trained animals.
source: This suggests that MUT-7 is required for the formation of the HPL-2-H3 complex in odor-trained animals but that it does not directly associate with either HPL-2 or histone H3.3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in mut-7 mutants.

claim: MUT-7 does not directly associate with either HPL-2 or histone H3.3.
source: This suggests that MUT-7 is required for the formation of the HPL-2-H3 complex in odor-trained animals but that it does not directly associate with either HPL-2 or histone H3.3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of BiFC signal between MUT-7 and HPL-2.

claim: Phosphorylated MUT-7 directs the heterochromatin complex to genetic loci, possibly using 22G RNA as a guide.
source: This led us to hypothesize that phosphorylated MUT-7 directs the heterochromatin complex to genetic loci, possibly using 22G RNA as a guide.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference from BiFC and other experimental results.

claim: The odor learning ability of hpl-2;Cewrn-1 double mutants was similar to the odor learning ability of Cewrn-1 or hpl-2 single-mutant animals.
source: We generated hpl-2;Cewrn-1 double mutants and found that the odor learning ability of the double mutants was similar to the odor learning ability of Cewrn-1 or hpl-2 single-mutant animals (Figure 1B, lower).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 act in the same pathway to promote learning.
source: The results indicate that CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 act in the same pathway to promote learning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis results.

claim: 80% of odor-trained worms co-expressing CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs showed reconstituted fluorescence in the AWC nucleus.
source: We co-expressed CeWRN-1 tagged with the N-terminal half of Venus and HPL-2 tagged with the C-terminal half of Venus in wild-type worms. We found that 80% of odor-trained worms but less than 4% of naïve worms showed reconstituted fluorescence in the AWC nucleus (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, eighth row; Figure 4C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Less than 4% of naïve worms co-expressing CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs showed reconstituted fluorescence in the AWC nucleus.
source: We co-expressed CeWRN-1 tagged with the N-terminal half of Venus and HPL-2 tagged with the C-terminal half of Venus in wild-type worms. We found that 80% of odor-trained worms but less than 4% of naïve worms showed reconstituted fluorescence in the AWC nucleus (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, eighth row; Figure 4C, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Less than 4% of naïve or odor-trained nrde-3(gg66) worms expressing CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 BiFC constructs exhibited the BiFC signal.
source: The same BiFC constructs were expressed in nrde-3(gg66), and less than 4% of naïve or odor-trained worms exhibited the BiFC signal (Figure 4D, third row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The association between HPL-2 and CeWRN-1 in odor-trained animals depends on NRDE-3.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that the association between HPL-2 and CeWRN-1 in odor-trained animals depends on NRDE-3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in nrde-3 mutants.

claim: Loss of CeWRN-1 reduced the BiFC signal between HIS-71 and HPL-2, as <7% of naïve and odor-trained worms showed fluorescence.
source: To determine whether CeWRN-1 affects HPL-2 binding to histone H3, we examined the BiFC of HIS-71 and HPL-2 in Cewrn-1(gk99) null mutants. We found that loss of CeWRN-1 reduced the BiFC signal, as <7% of naïve and odor-trained worms showed fluorescence (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, ninth row).
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CeWRN-1 is required for HPL-2 to associate with histone H3 in odor-trained animals.
source: These results showed that CeWRN-1 is required for HPL-2 to associate with histone H3 in odor-trained animals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the BiFC results in Cewrn-1 mutants.

claim: The human WRN protein associates with the heterochromatin-binding protein HP1 and histone H3K9me3 in a human WS mesenchymal stem cell model.
source: Our data were also consistent with the observation that the human WRN protein associates with the heterochromatin-binding protein HP1 and histone H3K9me3 in a human WS mesenchymal stem cell model (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: In Cewrn-1 loss-of-function mutants, odr-1 22G RNA levels did not change with odor training.
source: We found that in Cewrn-1 loss-of-function mutants, odr-1 22G RNA levels did not change (Figure 2C, seventh data set).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: odr-1 22G RNA expression at baseline was the same in wild-type worms and Cewrn-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, odr-1 22G RNA expression at baseline was the same in wild-type worms and Cewrn-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, left and right).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In mut-7(pk204) mutants, the odr-1 22G RNA level was significantly decreased in odor-trained animals.
source: By contrast, in mut-7(pk204) mutants, the odr-1 22G RNA level was significantly decreased in odor-trained animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous MUT-7 functions normally in the Cewrn-1 mutant background.
source: These results suggest that endogenous MUT-7 functions normally in the Cewrn-1 mutant background.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 22G RNA levels are normal in Cewrn-1 mutants.

claim: CeWRN-1 is required for HPL-2 to load onto histone H3 and fine tune gene expression via the small RNA-mediated silencing pathway in AWCs during butanone-related learning.
source: Taken together, the data imply that CeWRN-1 is required for HPL-2 to load onto histone H3 and thus fine tune gene expression via the small RNA-mediated silencing pathway in AWCs during the butanone-related learning process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined BiFC and RT-qPCR results.

claim: Loss of CeWRN-1 reduced the total brood size from an average of 213 in the wild type to 185 eggs in the Cewrn-1(gk99) mutant.
source: We found that loss of CeWRN-1 reduced the total brood size from an average of 213 in the wild type to 185 eggs in the Cewrn-1(gk99) mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by brood size data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of MUT-7 exonuclease activity greatly reduced brood size to an average of 96 eggs.
source: Loss of MUT-7 exonuclease activity greatly reduced brood size to an average of 96 eggs, and mut-7;Cewrn-1 double-mutant animals showed an average of only 68 eggs per brood.
evidence: The claim is supported by brood size data.

claim: mut-7;Cewrn-1 double-mutant animals showed an average of only 68 eggs per brood.
source: Loss of MUT-7 exonuclease activity greatly reduced brood size to an average of 96 eggs, and mut-7;Cewrn-1 double-mutant animals showed an average of only 68 eggs per brood.
evidence: The claim is supported by brood size data.

claim: The wild-type and Cewrn-1 mutant animals showed similar numbers of cell corpses per gonad arm.
source: The wild-type and Cewrn-1 mutant animals showed similar numbers of cell corpses per gonad arm, while the mut-7 mutants showed a larger number of cell corpses (Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell corpse counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: The mut-7 mutants showed a larger number of cell corpses per gonad arm compared to wild-type.
source: The wild-type and Cewrn-1 mutant animals showed similar numbers of cell corpses per gonad arm, while the mut-7 mutants showed a larger number of cell corpses (Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell corpse counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: The MUT-7 exonuclease is required for germ cell viability.
source: Thus, the MUT-7 exonuclease is required for germ cell viability, but the CeWRN-1 helicase may not be sufficient.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cell corpse and brood size data.

claim: The CeWRN-1 helicase may not be sufficient for germ cell viability.
source: Thus, the MUT-7 exonuclease is required for germ cell viability, but the CeWRN-1 helicase may not be sufficient.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference from the cell corpse and brood size data.

claim: The residues critical for 3'−5′ exonuclease catalytic activity are conserved between MUT-7 and the exonuclease domain of mammalian WRN.
source: The obtained molecular evidence of the WRN homolog's 3′−5′ exonuclease function indicates that the residues critical for 3'−5′ exonuclease catalytic activity are conserved between MUT-7 and the exonuclease domain of mammalian WRN (Ketting et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ketting et al., 1999.

claim: The human WRN protein exhibits both DNase and RNase activities.
source: The human WRN protein exhibits both DNase and RNase activities (Suzuki et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 1999.

claim: The WRN exonuclease and helicase domains are likely to cooperate in repairing DNA.
source: The analysis of the crystal structures of the WRN exonuclease and helicase domains indicated that they are likely to cooperate in repairing DNA (Perry et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perry et al., 2006.

claim: Nematode MUT-7 is involved in germline transposon silencing via the RNA interference pathway.
source: Nematode MUT-7 is involved in germline transposon silencing via the RNA interference pathway (Ketting et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ketting et al., 1999.

claim: Loss of MUT-7 results in the loss of transposon silencing and increased activity of the DNA repair machinery in response to transposon-mediated DNA double-strand breaks in germ cells.
source: Loss of MUT-7 results in the loss of transposon silencing and increased activity of the DNA repair machinery in response to transposon-mediated DNA double-strand breaks in germ cells (Wallis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wallis et al., 2019.

claim: The RNAi pathway silences transposon activity by producing abundant 22G RNAs in the nematode germline that serve to repress transposase expression.
source: Furthermore, the RNAi pathway silences transposon activity by producing abundant 22G RNAs in the nematode germline that serve to repress transposase expression (Gu et al., 2009; Halic and Moazed, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2009 and Halic and Moazed, 2009.

claim: Prolonged external stimulation of C. elegans activates 22G RNA synthesis via the function of MUT-7 in the cytoplasm.
source: Our work indicates that the prolonged external stimulation of C. elegans activates 22G RNA synthesis via the function of MUT-7 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: The entry of 22G RNA into the nucleus guides the interaction between CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 to form repressive chromatin.
source: Moreover, the entry of 22G RNA into the nucleus guides the interaction between CeWRN-1 and HPL-2 to form repressive chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: Some microRNAs, such as miR124, show differential expression in WS mouse models compared to wild-type mice.
source: Small RNAs involved in WS process have also been observed in WS mouse models, in which some microRNAs, such as miR124, show differential expression compared to that in wild-type mice (Dallaire et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dallaire et al., 2012.

claim: The synthesis and shuttling of siRNA into the AWC nucleus are required for CeWRN-1-dependent olfactory learning.
source: Although evidence of the importance of siRNA in WS is currently lacking, we systematically demonstrated in the present study that the synthesis and shuttling of siRNA into the AWC nucleus are required for CeWRN-1-dependent olfactory learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: Human WS may result from changes in epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation patterns rather than loss of genome integrity.
source: Indeed, a few recent reports indicate that human WS may result not from the loss of genome integrity but from changes in epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation patterns (Maierhofer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maierhofer et al., 2019.

claim: MUT-7 acts specifically in the cytoplasm to promote siRNA biogenesis.
source: MUT-7 acts specifically in the cytoplasm to promote siRNA biogenesis and in the nucleus to associate with CeWRN-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: MUT-7 acts in the nucleus to associate with CeWRN-1.
source: MUT-7 acts specifically in the cytoplasm to promote siRNA biogenesis and in the nucleus to associate with CeWRN-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: The import of siRNA by the nuclear Argonaute NRDE-3 promotes the loading of HPL-2 onto specific loci.
source: The import of siRNA by the nuclear Argonaute NRDE-3 promotes the loading of the heterochromatin-binding protein HP1 homolog HPL-2 onto specific loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: The heterochromatin complex represses the gene expression of the guanylyl cyclase ODR-1 to direct olfactory plasticity in C. elegans.
source: This heterochromatin complex represses the gene expression of the guanylyl cyclase ODR-1 to direct olfactory plasticity in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from this study.

claim: The exonuclease and helicase domains of human WRN may act in concert to promote RNA-dependent loading into a heterochromatin complex.
source: Our findings suggest that the exonuclease and helicase domains of human WRN may act in concert to promote RNA-dependent loading into a heterochromatin complex, and the failure of this entire process reduces plasticity in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference from the C. elegans data.

claim: The failure of RNA-dependent loading into a heterochromatin complex reduces plasticity in postmitotic neurons.
source: Our findings suggest that the exonuclease and helicase domains of human WRN may act in concert to promote RNA-dependent loading into a heterochromatin complex, and the failure of this entire process reduces plasticity in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the inference from the C. elegans data.

claim: Patients with WS have inactivating mutations in either the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain or the helicase domain of WRN.
source: Patients with WS have inactivating mutations in either the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain or the helicase domain of WRN (Yu et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 1996 and Huang et al., 2006.

claim: ~95% mutations in WRN genes produce frameshift and nonsense mutations that are predicted to result in truncated proteins.
source: First, although sequence analysis of individuals with WS shows that ~95% mutations in WRN genes produce frameshift and nonsense mutations that are predicted to result in truncated proteins, people harboring mutations causing a 90% reduction in WRN helicase activity but leaving WRN exonuclease activity intact do not present with the clinical manifestations of WS (Kamath-Loeb et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kamath-Loeb et al., 2017.

claim: People harboring mutations causing a 90% reduction in WRN helicase activity but leaving WRN exonuclease activity intact do not present with the clinical manifestations of WS.
source: First, although sequence analysis of individuals with WS shows that ~95% mutations in WRN genes produce frameshift and nonsense mutations that are predicted to result in truncated proteins, people harboring mutations causing a 90% reduction in WRN helicase activity but leaving WRN exonuclease activity intact do not present with the clinical manifestations of WS (Kamath-Loeb et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kamath-Loeb et al., 2017.

claim: In 10–15% of patients diagnosed with WS, no mutation is found within WRN.
source: Second, in 10–15% of patients diagnosed with WS, no mutation is found within WRN (Oshima and Hisama, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oshima and Hisama, 2014.

claim: In some non-classical WS cases, an arginine-to-cysteine substitution is found at amino acid 507 (R507C) in the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain of POLD.
source: In some of these non-classical cases, an arginine-to-cysteine substitution is found at amino acid 507 (R507C) in the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain of POLD, which is a DNA polymerase that associates with the WRN helicase during lagging strand synthesis (Lessel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lessel et al., 2015.

claim: POLD is a DNA polymerase that associates with the WRN helicase during lagging strand synthesis.
source: In some of these non-classical cases, an arginine-to-cysteine substitution is found at amino acid 507 (R507C) in the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain of POLD, which is a DNA polymerase that associates with the WRN helicase during lagging strand synthesis (Lessel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lessel et al., 2015.

claim: In a Drosophila melanogaster model of WS, loss of the Drosophila WRN affects lifespan under NAD+ supplementation.
source: Third, in a Drosophila melanogaster model of WS, loss of the Drosophila WRN, which only contains the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain, affects lifespan under NAD+ supplementation (Fang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fang et al., 2019.

claim: The Drosophila WRN only contains the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain.
source: Third, in a Drosophila melanogaster model of WS, loss of the Drosophila WRN, which only contains the 3′−5′ exonuclease domain, affects lifespan under NAD+ supplementation (Fang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fang et al., 2019.

claim: Fang et al., 2019 reported WRN-related microarray data in the C. elegans brain nervous system.
source: In addition, Fang et al., 2019 reported WRN-related microarray data in the C. elegans brain nervous system, and their findings suggest that WRN may play important roles in neuronal development and neuroplasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fang et al., 2019.

claim: WRN may play important roles in neuronal development and neuroplasticity.
source: In addition, Fang et al., 2019 reported WRN-related microarray data in the C. elegans brain nervous system, and their findings suggest that WRN may play important roles in neuronal development and neuroplasticity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the citation to Fang et al., 2019.

claim: AWC neurons respond to attractive volatile cues such as butanone.
source: The cells within the sensory circuit include amphid wing cells (termed AWC neurons), which respond to attractive volatile cues such as butanone (Bargmann et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bargmann et al., 1993.

claim: The nuclear accumulation of EGL-4 in odor-trained wild-type animals is required for olfactory learning and adaptation.
source: The nuclear accumulation of EGL-4 in odor-trained wild-type animals is required for olfactory learning and adaptation (L'Etoile et al., 2002; O'Halloran et al., 2009; O'Halloran et al., 2012; Cho et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to L'Etoile et al., 2002; O'Halloran et al., 2009; O'Halloran et al., 2012; and Cho et al., 2016.
